newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: FEATURE - Zimbabwe sees ray of hope for economy.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Zimbabwe sees ray of hope for economy.

text.p: Zimbabwe finally seems to be winning the fight against years of high inflation and interest rates, but continued deficit spending could still bar its return to a crucial IMF support deal this year.

President Robert Mugabe's government is blamed by economic analysts for high spending which kept the country in an upward inflation spiral during the five-year reform plan just ended, pushing percentage interest rates into the high 20s.
The government repeatedly missed inflation targets set by the Western-backed plan, which was adopted in 1991 to jump-start an economy stunted by a decade of flirting with socialism.

Last September, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bankm, which marshalled international donor aid for the first phase of the structural adjustment programme, decided to suspend crucial balance of payments support to Zimbabwe.

Now, as the country prepares to launch a second tranche of reforms this year, inflation and interest rates are falling, kindling hope that industry strangled by debt can resume growing, with renewed donor support.
Zimbabwe's year-on-year consumer price inflation fell to a three-year low of 17.7 percent in August from 22 percent in July, largely due to cheaper food.
"A drop in inflation of this magnitude is to be welcomed and throws a new light on the investment markets and the conduct of monetary policy," said market and economic analyst Charles Gurney.
Inflation has fallen from a peak of 28 percent in January.

The central Reserve Bank and economic analysts expect higher fuel and milk prices to push it back up in the next two months, but they forecast an end-of-year rate of 20 percent, dipping to 17 percent by next June.
SOFTER MONEY MARKET RATES HELPED STOCK EXCHANGE BOOM
Money market rates have been softening since the beginning of the year, tracking down to a range of 22 and 23 percent in the last few weeks from around 29 percent in January.

This has contributed to a boom on the local stock exchange as investors desert the money market to chase higher yields on the bourse. Zimbabwe's industrial stock index soared 80.7 percent over the first nine months of the year.
At the start of August, commercial banks lowered their minimum lending rates by up to 2.5 percentage points, to 30 percent.

In mid-August the central Reserve Bank sliced two percentage points from its rediscount rate, to 27.5 percent. The cut was the bank's first rate cut in two years, stoking hopes that commercial banks would lower their lending rates further.

"Producer price trends and the underlying rate of inflation show that inflationary pressures in the economy may now be relenting," said Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe governor Leonard Tsumba in a policy statement.

Reinforcing efforts to keep up the downward pressure on inflation, Tsumba announced a number of measures to contain money supply growth, which he said had remained persistently above the target of 22 percent per year and threatened to refuel inflation.
Among the measures:

-- All foreign currency accounts would be eligible for a 17.5 percent reserve requirement in Zimbabwe dollars and the central bank would, beginning in September, pay for gold purchases in foreign currency.

-- The Reserve Bank would accommodate unsecured overnight advances (for accounting errors only) for banks and discount houses up to Z$1 million (US$ 100,000). Beyond that level, it would demand a formal explanation and justification of error.

-- The bank would also only accommodate changes in discount house call money deposits. Discount houses used to accept deposits which Tsumba said should ordinarily be deposited with banks and therefore attract statutory reserves. This, he said, tended to weaken the statutory reserve ratio and eroded efforts to curb the growth in money supply.

"These measures, together with current open market operations, will ensure that money supply grows at no more than 22 percent per annum, sufficient to support private sector credit growth of at least 20 percent," Tsumba said.
"We are finally getting in the right direction and this is an element of getting back on the IMF programme," independent economic analyst Eric Bloch told Reuters.
The government is expected to open serious talks on a new financial programme with the IMF and the World Bank in October.
GOVERNMENT MUST CURB DOMESTIC BORROWING, CUT BUDGET DEFICIT

However, Bloch and other analysts warn that even a sustained fall in inflation and tighter control of money supply could be rendered ineffective if the government failed to curb its domestic borrowings and bring down the budget deficit.
"What is of far greater importance is to satisfy the IMF that we are going to reduce the deficit. So far there has not been a single year where we have brought it down to target," Bloch points out.

Under the first phase of ambitious reforms, which ended last year, the government set out to halve its budget deficit, to five percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by the fiscal year 1994/95 from 10.4 percent in 1990/91.
Instead, the deficit ended up at 13.4 percent of GDP in 1994/95. In the 1995/96 fiscal year ended June 30, it was pegged at 10.1 percent, compared to a revised target of 6.7 percent.
The government now says it intends to lower the deficit to 8.5 percent of GDP in the current financial year ending June 30.

But economic analysts Bloch and Gurney are sceptical. They point to recent salary hikes of 20 percent awarded to striking civil servants in August -- increases over and above a nine percent rise they received in July.
That leaves the government looking for an extra Z$1.4 billion not forecast in the 1996/97 wage bill.
If this sum is borrowed from the domestic market, it would swell the budget deficit over the 8.5 percent target.
Bloch and Anthony Hawkins, business studies professor at Harare's University of Zimbabwe, estimate the deficit would rise to between 10 and 12.5 percent in 1996/97.

In addition, they say that if the government resorts to further domestic borrowing this could drive interest rates up and crowd out the private sector, which was starting to sound positive about borrowing rates after years of complaining they were punitively high.
Gurney also criticises the government for hosting a costly World Solar Summit in September -- an event which provoked loud complaints of irresponsible spending.
"Sustained economic stability is not possible without a rational fiscal policy and until this is sorted out, we must expect price and interest rate volatility," Gurney said.
Bloch feels things are "moving in the right direction", but cautioned: "What's critical for us is to convince the IMF that we are going to stick to that direction."
